An affair with an economist exposed the calculus of modern dating.

By Merritt Tierce

We met on OkCupid. In the same week as we read new predictions of an imminent intelligence explosion, Elon Musk reminds us that intelligence is an elusive concept. In a live interview he confidently asserted that America was behind the overthrow of Ukraine’s pro-Russian government in 2014. The most cursory investigation - a mere Grok query - would have shown him that this isn’t true; that it is a myth propagated by Russia and its useful idiots.

If Musk often finds that rumours are too good to check, that’s because his brain is optimised for profitable action, not accuracy. He is highly intelligent, of course, but he didn’t build trillion-dollar businesses by carefully weighing evidence and discounting for biases. That would only have got in the way of what he wanted to do. Rather than coolly assessing reality, he sets about it with hammer and chisel. He and Jensen Huang are the archetypal unreasonable men on whom progress depends. (I say this unironically, by the way. Nobody would be landing rockets without Musk being mad enough to believe he could make them.)

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, has a different temperament to Musk or Huang. Where they are impulsive and volatile, he is systematic and logical. He writes long, lucid essays which make sober arguments. He weighs different scenarios, calculates trade-offs. He sweats over the ethics of AI. He has given Claude its own “constitution”. He employs philosophers, something it is merely funny to imagine Jensen Huang doing. He doesn’t come across as blatantly self-serving or quick to dissemble - but maybe that’s why we should be sceptical of him. Everyone expects Musk and to a lesser extent Huang to believe preposterous things, and so we discount for it. Amodei reaches his positions honestly and methodically. That doesn’t mean they’re not crazy.

In the week of Anthropic’s IPO, the New York Times has published a piece about the company’s internal culture, by the excellent Jasmine Sun. Sun spoke to current and former employees to find out how Amodei and his staff really think about the company’s mission. Many of them were about to become enormously rich. She found them unexcited by this prospect. They worked six days a week, twelve hours a day, and lived relatively spartan lives. They found it hard to think about what they might spend their money on. They were also weighed down by the responsibility of building a product they believe may well take over the world, with radically uncertain consequences for humanity.

Amodei has created a company in the image of himself. He is, as far as I can tell, idealistic, thoughtful, and concerned to do the right thing. His staff think and talk like him and share his beliefs about the future. Notwithstanding some emerging differences of opinion over corporate strategy, the company is very unified. This is in contrast to OpenAI, which, in the image of its CEO, has a hyper-political culture, riven by warring factions. That sounds bad, but I’m starting to wonder if an AI lab in which everyone shares the same mission and mindset might actually be more dangerous than one in which everyone is trying to undermine each other.

Sun’s piece identifies three assumptions on which Anthropic’s strategy rests. One is that the AI race is inevitable: a superintelligent AI is going to get built, whether Anthropic participates or not. A second is that whichever company builds this AI will possess enormous power. As a former employee puts it, it will control “the most dangerous cyberweapons in the world, the cures and recipes for every disease, and an army of tireless digital geniuses to do its bidding.” Amodei is said to believe that Anthropic may become more powerful than the US government and ought to start building relationships with nation states.

The third assumption can be framed as an answer to the question posed by the first two. Given that this thing is going to get built, and given it will be unprecedentedly powerful, then who should control it? Sam Altman? Mark Zuckerberg? Xi Jinping? Duh - it has to be us: Anthropic. We’re the good guys. Ergo, in the absence of collective action imposed by government, it is our duty to build AI as fast as possible.

This logic explains why Amodei is making cataclysmic predictions of AI’s impact on jobs while doing his utmost to advance it. It’s why, at the same time as he calls for government help in “pacing the frontier”, he is also focused on “racing to the top” - on building AI systems so superior that they force the rest of the industry to adopt its standards of safety. In Sun’s paraphrase: “Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.”

There is a striking and somewhat unlikely coincidence of priorities here. Normally, we would expect commercial and social goals to be in conflict with each other, to some extent. That’s why we make businesses subject to laws and regulations. Amodei believes - I think genuinely - that he is pursuing wealth, power and public good all at the same time. Long and earnest reflection has convinced him that he has a moral imperative to build a multi-trillion-dollar company which is more powerful than governments.

I mean, that smells funny, doesn’t it?

Each of the assumptions on which Amodei’s strategy rests is questionable, but it is the third which seems most dubious. Why should we trust Anthropic to use its power for good? Come to that, why does Amodei trust himself to be a wise, all-powerful steward of civilisation? In the West, after a few hundred years of trials and errors, we concluded that kings should be tightly constrained or abolished. The logic of “this time is different” may apply to this revolutionary technology, but unless human nature is about to undergo a comparable leap forward, it seems unlikely that one man or one company can acquire so much power without using it for authoritarian and destructive ends.

To be fair to Amodei, he is calling on Congress to permit AI companies to coordinate a slowdown without falling foul of competition law. That could be construed as self-interested, too, of course, although I don’t believe he is Machiavellian. I think he looks into his heart and sees only good intentions. Anthropic employees look at him, and at each other, and see the same. But over time, his good intentions always converge with the maximisation of wealth and power. It was out of good intentions that Amodei held the release of Claude back in 2022 on safety grounds, letting ChatGPT go first. It was also out of good intentions that he then decided Anthropic should try and race ahead of OpenAI.

As Sun points out, there is a parallel with the technology here. We cannot parse the inner workings of LLMs, which means we can’t tell if they’re on our side or merely faking compliance. We can only observe their behaviour and adjust their constraints accordingly. Similarly, we cannot be sure whether or not a particular CEO or company is or will always be altruistic. But given everything we’ve learned from history, we ought to proceed on the basis that, under intense competitive pressure, they will choose what’s right for them over what’s right for society.

This returns us to the slipperiness of “intelligence”. You can be highly intelligent and believe false or impossible things. Highly driven people subordinate their rational faculty to their desires. Clever people are particularly good at rationalising their self-deceptions. Amodei is highly driven and very clever, but if he were wise he would not trust himself. He would take what Daniel Kahneman called the outside view, look at the base rate of how powerful leaders behave under pressure, and ask how likely it is that he will be at the far end of the distribution or off the edge of it. If that seems implausible, then his own predictions about AI imply that even a coordinated slowdown wouldn’t go nearly far enough. A more radical constraint on Anthropic’s power will be necessary.

Simply put, if any AI company were to become even half as powerful as Amodei predicts, we should want it under public control. Not because governments are wise, but because in a democracy, great power must be answerable to the people. This seems quite likely to happen anyway, one way or another. The more powerful that Anthropic or another lab becomes, the more it will come into conflict with the state. You can’t have two Leviathans. Anthropic’s skirmishes with the Pentagon were interpreted in the context of MAGA, but after Hegseth and Trump are gone, the government will still need to show that it is in charge, whoever occupies the White House. I wonder if Anthropic’s shareholders have this factored into their valuation of the company.

Either way, what Amodei and his co-founders have built in six years is astonishing. I don’t want to be too hard on him (especially if he’s going to be World-King). He is a business leader who thinks deeply about ethics and engages in argument and debate. That is good. I’m just wary of relentless, systematic reasoners who are convinced of their own correctness, especially when they are creating powerful entities which think like them. “It is not the slumber of reason that engenders monsters,” wrote Deleuze and Guattari in 1972, “but vigilant and insomniac rationality.” Insomniac rationality - what a way to describe Anthropic, and the machine it’s building.

The falcon cannot hear the falconer;

Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold;

Mere anarchy is loosed upon the world,

The blood-dimmed tide is loosed, and everywhere

The best lack all conviction, while the worst

The wars at our borders, the climate crisis, the raging industrial revolution, rapidly shifting and unpredictable international relations, the pandemic and its underlying causes that will lead to a recurrence if not addressed: humanity is in a position to tackle and overcome all of these. The radical step of creating rule of law based inescapable interdependencies across national borders, proved incredibly effective and successful. This day and age, with our main security guarantor going rogue and openly embracing our adversary, asks for a quantum leap in deepening, strengthening and widening the successful formula of European integration. Out of naked self-interest and for the many, not the few. So that the center may hold and hold firm.

There was a period in my career at Facebook when I REALLY felt I deserved a promotion to director.

I thought about it often. I felt frustrated and overlooked. I spent what felt like years being mad about this title.

And when I finally got the promotion, I was basically like, “Whatever. Too late.”

You wanna know what’s crazy?

Since leaving Facebook, no one has ever asked me what my title was there.

What mattered about that period of my career was that I got to work at an extraordinary company during an insane period of growth. I got to solve problems I’d never seen before, learn from incredibly talented people, and develop skills that have served me for the rest of my career.

BUT.

I’ve also had the opposite experience. Years later, when I got my first C-level title, COO, I watched the world treat me differently almost overnight.

Different people took my calls. I got invited into different rooms. Opportunities showed up that hadn’t before.

So which is it? Do titles matter or not?

That’s one of the questions I wanted to explore in this week’s WorkLife episode, the third in our series on How to Get What You Want at Work.

I interviewed my friend Gokul Rajaram, who has had a remarkable career in tech. He’s worked at Google, Facebook, Square, and DoorDash, and he’s also become an incredibly successful investor.

I’ve known Gokul for years, and one of the things I’ve always admired about him is how deliberately he’s made career choices.

Despite being one of the most accomplished product leaders I know, Gokul has never had the chief product officer title. He’s been recruited for it many times; he’s just never taken it. He is also one of the least title-motivated people I know, and he’s written a whole thing about how companies should delay giving out titles for as long as possible.

His argument isn’t that titles are entirely meaningless. It’s that people often give up things that matter much more in order to get them.

Gokul thinks about his career the way he thinks about investing. He cares a lot more about what a decision will be worth ten years from now than how impressive it looks today.

Listen to this episode

A theme keeps coming up in this series: when you think about your career as a ladder, you’re constantly focused on the next rung. The next promotion, the next title, the next bump in comp. Progress is pretty easy to measure. As Simone pointed out in the first episode, focusing on the ladder can make you lose sight of what you actually want. Gokul’s point is slightly different: focusing on the next rung can distract you from building something much more valuable over the long term.

And I think that’s the point: Titles can be valuable without being particularly good measures of career success.

They can change how people perceive you. I’ve experienced that firsthand, and I think that matters particularly for people whose authority isn’t automatically assumed.

But when you’re choosing a job, optimizing for a title can mean sacrificing things that will matter much more to your career five or ten years down the road.

So what should you focus on instead?

Gokul’s answer is emphatic: the company you’re joining. When I asked him whether he’d take a bigger title at a mediocre company or a smaller role at a company with extraordinary potential, he said, “1,000 out of 1,000 times, always choose company.”

I definitely lived this at Google and Facebook. When a company is growing that quickly, you get opportunities to do things you never would have imagined. New problems show up, your responsibilities change, and suddenly you’re learning things you might have waited years to learn somewhere else.

There’s a famous saying in tech: “If you’re offered a seat on a rocketship, you don’t ask which seat; you just get on.”

Gokul’s top three priorities when choosing a job are:

  • Company trajectory: How quickly is the company growing, and where is it headed?

  • Talent density: Will you be surrounded by extraordinary people you can learn from?

  • Scope and experience: What will you own, and what will you learn?

Titles and compensation come further down his list.

He’s not suggesting you work for nothing. He thinks your compensation should be fair and sufficient to support your life. But beyond that, he argues you should prioritize the things that will build your career’s value over the long term.

So, I’ll start by saying I basically agree. Particularly early in your career, there's enormous value in finding a company that's going places, surrounding yourself with brilliant people, and throwing yourself into the experience.

AND it is so much harder in practice than it sounds.

There are a couple of reasons why:

1. Rocketships explode.

Earlier this year, I wrote an entire essay about why picking rocketships is a bad career strategy. And I still basically believe that, although Gokul is making me rethink the phrasing.

Even venture capitalists, whose entire job is to identify promising companies, know they’re making bets. They spend enormous amounts of time evaluating companies and still expect many of their investments not to work out.

The difference is that VCs have portfolios. Most of us have one job at a time, and we’re investing years of our lives in it.

Which is why I loved how Gokul evaluated leaving Facebook to join Square.

Square was an exciting startup, but it was also risky. So he asked himself a question I’ve actually been asking people for years when they’re considering new jobs:

If this company fails in two years, will I still be glad I took the job?

Watch on YouTube

He literally wrote down what he’d get to learn and experience: leading a much bigger team, building a payments product at enormous scale, and being part of the management team.

Even if Square failed, he decided those experiences would make the move worthwhile.

If you’ve read my rocketship article, you know I believe strongly in this exercise. So yes, try to pick a rocketship. Getting on one can change your entire career. But recognize that you’re making a bet, and make sure the decision is worth it even if the bet doesn’t pay off.

2. It’s surprisingly easy to over-optimize for one thing.

One of the worst career decisions I’ve made was a job I took almost entirely because I was excited about the people involved. I believed in them, wanted to work with them, and didn’t spend nearly enough time evaluating the trajectory of the company itself.

Listening to Gokul made me think back on that decision and others I’ve made throughout my career. It’s so easy to get excited about one aspect of an opportunity — the people, the title, the compensation — that you don’t look critically enough at everything else.

And the tricky thing is that these are all perfectly legitimate things to care about! The people you work with matter enormously. Titles can open doors. Compensation matters, both for your financial security and for the choices it gives you.

But it's easy to get so excited about one of those things that you stop asking hard questions about the others.

I think that’s part of what makes Gokul’s approach so useful. He’s forcing you to think about the whole opportunity, especially what that opportunity will be worth to you five or ten years from now. Even if it means giving up something that feels really important today.

One of my favorite things Gokul said during our conversation was:

Gokul talked about the difference between short-term compensation and long-term wealth. And I think there’s a version of that distinction that applies to our careers more broadly.

The wealth you’re building over the course of your career isn’t just financial. It’s also the skills, experiences, relationships, and reputation that give you more choices about what you want to do with your life ten or twenty years from now.

And when I look back at my time at Facebook, I spent so much energy being mad about not getting promoted to director that I barely noticed the extraordinary foundation I was building for the rest of my career.

Titles matter. They open doors, confer authority, and sometimes give you access to opportunities you wouldn’t otherwise have.

But if you spend all your energy optimizing for the things that make you feel successful today, you can end up under-optimizing for the career and life you actually want in the long run.

Stilte is een voorwaarde om te kunnen spreken. Zonder stilte is er nauwelijks ruimte om te luisteren. En zonder luisteren zijn woorden geen aanspreken meer, hooguit informatie. Ik vroeg me af wat dat betekent voor gewoon, alledaags contact. Hoe vaak vullen we een stilte meteen op, terwijl de ander misschien nog aan het zoeken is naar woorden? En wat zou er gebeuren als we die stilte gewoon even laten duren, zonder alvast te bedenken wat er gezegd moet worden?

Elkaar opnieuw ontmoeten

We’ve lost you again. Om die onbedoelde dubbele bodem van deze zin in deze context, moest ik stilletjes lachen. We kunnen elkaar kwijtraken terwijl we de hele dag met elkaar in contact staan. We kunnen denken dat we iemand goed begrijpen, terwijl die ander zich er steeds minder in herkent. En soms merken we pas hoe ver we iemand kwijt zijn, op het moment dat diegene zegt: ik voel me al zo lang niet meer gehoord.

De onderzoekers van deze dag wezen elk een eigen richting. Husserl laat zien waarom je de ervaring van een ander nooit helemaal kunt zien. Levinas herinnert ons aan de Ander die ons begrip te boven gaat en ons tot verantwoordelijkheid roept. En de gesprekken over eenzaamheid lieten zien wat er gebeurt als mensen elkaar geen ruimte meer geven om anders te zijn dan verwacht.

Wellicht begint daar een nieuw gesprek. Een gesprek waarin we erkennen dat de ander meer is dan alles wat we inmiddels over hem weten. We kunnen van elkaar houden en elkaar nooit helemaal kennen. Iemand kan veranderen zonder dat je dat meteen begrijpt of zelfs herkent. Samenleven vraagt dat we dat verdragen, en elkaar de vrijheid gunnen om opnieuw te verschijnen. Ook na vele jaren. Of misschien dan juist het meest.

Luisteren met Levinas is een door lezers gesteunde publicatie. Wil je nieuwe posts ontvangen en mijn werk steunen? Overweeg dan om gratis of betalende abonnee te worden.

Delen

Je kunt je werkrollen vergelijken met jassen. Sommige zitten heerlijk, andere zijn te warm of zwaar. Vaak kies je een jas zelf, maar soms krijg je een jas aangereikt. En vooral: welke jas trek je bijna automatisch aan, welke jas kan even in de kast en welke zou je de komende tijd wel vaker willen dragen?

Welke jassen hangen aan jouw kapstok?

In ons werk vervullen we de hele tijd allerlei rollen. Soms heel bewust, maar vaak ook automatisch. Manon Ruijters maakt in het interview Stevig (leren) staan een interessant onderscheid tussen je professionele identiteit en de rollen die je vervult.

Je professionele identiteit gaat over wie je bent als professional: wat je belangrijk vindt, waar je voor staat en hoe je van betekenis wilt zijn in je werk. De rollen die je vervult, zijn manieren waarop je daar in de praktijk invulling aan geeft. Je kunt bijvoorbeeld graag anderen helpen, maar dat betekent niet dat je altijd de rol van probleemoplosser op je hoeft te nemen.

Rollen kun je oppakken, anders invullen of weer neerleggen. Je bént niet je rol. Juist daarom is het interessant om eens met wat afstand naar je eigen rollen te kijken. De metafoor van jassen kan wel helpen. Welke jas trek je graag aan en zit heerlijk? Welke jas is nu misschien iets te warm? Welke jas heb je ooit van iemand gekregen maar past toch niet heel goed? En welke jas kan even naar de zomerberging?

Met deze prompt krijg je zicht op jouw kapstok met werkrollen, ontdek je welke jassen je best vlot aantrekt en krijg je meer zicht op jassen die je wel vaker wilt dragen of bij de volgende kledingbeurs wil ruilen :-)

Wanneer kun je dit toepassen?

  • Als je merkt dat je steeds dezelfde rol oppakt, maar je vraagt je af of die rol eigenlijk wel bij jou hoort.

  • Als je een nieuwe rol hebt gekregen, bijvoorbeeld als projectleider, en zoekt naar een invulling die past bij wie jij bent als professional.

  • Als je merkt dat bepaalde rollen je veel energie kosten, terwijl je weinig toekomt aan de rollen die je energie geven

  • Als je bewuster wilt kiezen hoe je werkt: welke verantwoordelijkheden wil je zelf oppakken, welke kun je anders invullen en welke wil je misschien aan iemand anders overlaten?

Voorbeeldprompt

Help me ontdekken welke rollen ik in mijn werk op me neem en of ik die bewust kies. Gebruik de metafoor van een kapstok met jassen. Sommige zitten heerlijk, andere zijn te zwaar, blijven ongebruikt of heb ik van iemand anders gekregen.

Verken mijn werkgarderobe

Stel me maximaal drie scherpe vragen, één voor één, over mijn afgelopen werkweek. Wacht steeds op mijn antwoord. Onderzoek daarbij:

  • Welke rol trek ik bijna automatisch aan? Wat maakt dat ik die zelf oppak, terwijl iemand anders dat misschien ook kan?

  • Welke rol kreeg te weinig aandacht, terwijl die belangrijk is voor hoe ik mijn werk wil doen?

  • Welke rol verwachten anderen van mij, en wil ik die eigenlijk wel vervullen?

Reageer op mijn antwoorden, vraag waar nodig kritisch door en help me patronen herkennen. Geef daarna vier tot zes rollen korte, herkenbare namen. Laat me controleren of ze kloppen.

Maak mijn kapstok zichtbaar

Maak daadwerkelijk een warme, handgetekende illustratie van een houten kapstok met mijn verschillende jassen. Teken duidelijk verschillende soorten jassen, passend bij de rollen: bijvoorbeeld een kleurrijk jasje, een zware winterjas, een nette mantel of een comfortabele jas.

Hang aan elke jas een klein kaartje met één handgeschreven woord: de naam van de rol. Gebruik aquarel en potlood, met warme kleuren.

Toon alleen de kapstok met de jassen en hun kaartjes. Geen titel, stappen, uitleg of andere tekst. Laat me de afbeelding bekijken voordat we verdergaan.

Help me bewust kiezen

Vraag welke jas mijn aandacht trekt en waarom. Help me onderzoeken of ik die wil behouden, vaker aantrekken, anders invullen of doorgeven.

Stel maximaal twee verdiepende vragen. Daag me uit als ik iets vanzelfsprekend vind. Help me daarna één klein, concreet werkexperiment voor de komende week bedenken.

Houd het gesprek persoonlijk, vlot en nieuwsgierig. Gebruik geen stapnummers of vraagnummers in onze dialoog. Geef tussendoor inzichten, maar trek geen voorbarige conclusies.

Begin met je eerste vraag.

Aan de slag!

Denk terug aan je afgelopen werkweek. Wat vond je heerlijk om te doen? Wat heb je laten liggen? AI helpt je met een paar vragen om een paar rollen te ontdekken en geeft ze een naam. Vervolgens maakt het een afbeelding van jouw kapstok, met voor iedere rol een andere jas.

Kies één jas die je wilt houden, anders invullen, vaker aantrekken of misschien wel doorgeven. Laat AI je vervolgens helpen om een klein experiment te bedenken voor de komende werkweek.

Mijn ervaringen

Ik heb de prompt natuurlijk ook zelf gebruikt. Ik heb wel een beetje een ‘rollen’puzzel want in één project ben ik projectleider. Een rol die ik qua naam niet zo bij mij associeer. Ik wist het natuurlijk en ik merk dat ik nog wel zoekende ben naar hoe ik die rol invul. Ik hou van maken, uitwerken, experimenteren. en ben minder goed in tijdspaden in de gaten houden of een financeel overzicht maken (weet Joitske alles van).

Dus aan de slag met de prompt! Er kwamen 4 jassen uit: de ontwerper, de schrijver, de adviseur en de projectleider. Wat ik wel leuk vind aan deze oefening, is dat ik de jas van projectleider wat meer invulling heb gegeven. Een invulling die best bij me kan passen. Ik heb de jas wat passender gemaakt.

Reflectievraag

Welke jas trek jij bijna automatisch aan? En wat zou er veranderen als je de volgende keer bewust een andere keuze maakt?
